## Pre-Lab
1. Equation that relates $n$, $\theta$, $d$ and $\lambda$
   $$d sin(\theta) = n \lambda$$

1. Solving for 4000 and 440
   
$$d\sin(\theta) = n\lambda$$
$$\theta = \arcsin\left(\frac{n\lambda}{d}\right)$$
$$d = \frac{1\text{ cm}}{4000} = \frac{0.01\text{ m}}{4000}$$
$$d = 2.5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}$$
$$n = 1$$
$$\lambda = 0.44 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}$$
$$\theta = \arcsin\left(\frac{1 \times 0.44 \times 10^{-6}}{2.5 \times 10^{-6}}\right)$$
$$\theta = \arcsin(0.176)$$
$$\theta \approx 10.14^\circ$$
   

## Preamble 

The entire experiment was recorded and data interpolated
in python. Here is simple helper functions and imports.

These can mostly be ignored.

```{python}
import warnings
from math import log, pi, sqrt

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy import constants, odr
from scipy.stats import norm
from uncertainties import UFloat, ufloat, umath

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=FutureWarning, module="uncertainties")
warnings.filterwarnings(
    "ignore",
    category=FutureWarning,
    message=r"AffineScalarFunc\.__abs__\(\) is deprecated",
)
warnings.filterwarnings(
    "ignore", category=UserWarning, message="Using UFloat objects with std_dev==0"
)


def fit_odr(x: list[UFloat], y: list[UFloat], zero_intercept: bool = False):
    x_nom, x_err = [v.n for v in x], [v.s for v in x]
    y_nom, y_err = [v.n for v in y], [v.s for v in y]
    data = odr.RealData(x_nom, y_nom, sx=x_err, sy=y_err)
    if zero_intercept:
        model, beta0 = odr.Model(lambda p, x: p[0] * x), [1]
    else:
        model, beta0 = odr.Model(lambda p, x: p[0] * x + p[1]), [1, 0]
    out = odr.ODR(data, model, beta0=beta0).run()
    slope = ufloat(out.beta[0], out.sd_beta[0])
    intercept = (
        ufloat(out.beta[1], out.sd_beta[1]) if not zero_intercept else ufloat(0, 0)
    )
    y_pred = model.fcn(out.beta, np.array(x_nom))
    ss_res = np.sum((np.array(y_nom) - y_pred) ** 2)
    ss_tot = np.sum(
        np.array(y_nom) ** 2
        if zero_intercept
        else (np.array(y_nom) - np.mean(y_nom)) ** 2
    )
    r_squared = 1 - ss_res / ss_tot
    return slope, intercept, r_squared


def compsigma(a, b):
    return abs((a.n - b.n) / ((((a.s**2) + (b.s**2)) ** (1 / 2))))


def plot(
    x,
    y,
    fitodr=None,
    title="default title",
    xlabel="default xlabel",
    ylabel="default ylabel",
    show=True,
):
    if fitodr is None:
        fitodr = fit_odr(x, y)
    slope, intercept, r_squared = fitodr
    plt.figure()
    first = x[0].n
    last = x[-1].n

    plt.plot(
        [first, last],
        [first * slope.n + intercept.n, last * slope.n + intercept.n],
        "r-",
        label=f"Fit: $y = ({slope.n:.4g})x + ({intercept.n:.4g}),R^2 = {r_squared:.4f}$",
    )

    plt.errorbar(
        [v.nominal_value for v in x],
        [v.nominal_value for v in y],
        xerr=[v.std_dev for v in x],
        yerr=[v.std_dev for v in y],
        capsize=5,
        linestyle="none",
        marker="o",
        markersize=3,
        label="Data",
    )

    plt.title(title)
    plt.xlabel(xlabel)
    plt.ylabel(ylabel)
    plt.legend()
    if show:
        plt.show()


def plot_residuals(
    x,
    y,
    fitodr=None,
    title="Residuals",
    xlabel="default xlabel",
    ylabel="Residual (y - fit)",
    show=True,
):
    if fitodr is None:
        fitodr = fit_odr(x, y)
    slope, intercept, r_squared = fitodr
    residuals = [yi - (slope * xi + intercept) for xi, yi in zip(x, y)]
    sigma_eff = [
        sqrt(yi.std_dev**2 + (slope.n * xi.std_dev) ** 2) for xi, yi in zip(x, y)
    ]
    chi2 = sum((r.nominal_value**2) / (s**2) for r, s in zip(residuals, sigma_eff))
    dof = len(y) - 1
    chi2_reduced = chi2 / dof
    zero_fit = (
        ufloat(0, 0),
        ufloat(0, 0),
        0.0,
    )  # was None — plot()'s label needs a float

    plot(
        x,
        residuals,
        fitodr=zero_fit,
        title=f"{title} ($\\chi^2_\\nu = {chi2_reduced:.3f}$)",
        xlabel=xlabel,
        ylabel=ylabel,
        show=show,
    )

    return chi2_reduced


def two_tailed_p(diff: float):
    z = abs(diff)
    return 2 * norm.sf(z)
```


## Experiment 1

### Aim

To experimentaly determine some material through the use of
a spectrometer.

### Method

At the collimator end of a mass spectrometer, we first place our known mercury
source gas emitter lamp. 

We then recorded the first angle on both sides for any slit. 
We will average out the reading to find the center.

We then replace the mercury with an unknown source gas emitter
lamp. We record the slits with the brightest slits, so as to
choose the first order frequencies, this was done with our own discretion, rather than
objective source of reasoning.

We repeat this for all of the unknown source gas emitters.

This was all recorded in the dark.

### Results

The uncertainty in our angles was chosen to be 7.5 minutes.
The spectrometer had big notches of minutes as 15 minutes.
We attempted to record accurate to each minute, but we
choose the uncertainty as half the big notches since the
difficulty of reading a spectrometer in the dark.

```{python}
uncertainty = 7.5 / 60
middle = umath.radians(  # pyright: ignore[reportAttributeAccessIssue]
    (ufloat(40 + 7 / 60, uncertainty) + ufloat(12 + 11 / 60, uncertainty)) / 2
)
unknown1 = [41 + 49 / 60, 43 + 55 / 60, 47]
unknown2 = [48 + 55 / 60, 48, 47 + 15 / 60]
unknown3 = [47]
```

Math time
$d \sin{\theta} = n \lambda$
since we are trying to find the strongest lights, we can
assume n = 1.

our diffraction grating is 600 per mm, so we do 1mm divided
by our 600. d = 1e-3 / 600

$\frac{1 \times 10^-3}{600 \times 1} \sin{\theta} = \lambda$
So we do that, we define a calc wavelength function that
takes theta as its parameter, which we can reuse and solve
for unknown waves

```{python}
def calc_wavelength(x: UFloat):
    D = 1e-3 / 600
    return D * umath.sin(x)  # type: ignore


unknown1rad = [ufloat(np.deg2rad(x), np.deg2rad(uncertainty)) for x in unknown1]
unknown2rad = [ufloat(np.deg2rad(x), np.deg2rad(uncertainty)) for x in unknown2]
unknown3rad = [ufloat(np.deg2rad(x), np.deg2rad(uncertainty)) for x in unknown3]

unknown1waves = [calc_wavelength(x - middle) for x in unknown1rad]
unknown2waves = [calc_wavelength(x - middle) for x in unknown2rad]
unknown3waves = [calc_wavelength(x - middle) for x in unknown3rad]
[print(x) for x in unknown1waves]
pass
```

### Conclusions

Using some python manipulation, we can find the most
similarly matching for each wave.

This is programmer pilled but we compsigma to all the
spectral lines for each wavelength, we then sort that and
pick only the top n.


```{python}
# Just wanted to mention no ai was used ;3
def gettopwaves(unknown):
    return sorted(
        [
            [
                (compsigma(ufloat(spectral[0] / 1e9, 1e-15), wave), spectral[1])
                for spectral in spectral_lines
            ]
            for wave in unknown
        ]
    )


def getn(unknown, n):
    return [sorted(x, key=lambda x: x[0])[0:n] for x in gettopwaves(unknown)]
```

Simpy we can use this function. 
```{python}
[print(x) for x in getn(unknown1waves, 3)]
pass
```

For unknown one, for each slit we measured, helium appears
in the top three matches all three times, so its likely
helium.

We will use the function again for 3, we skip 2 and come
back later.

```{python}
pass
```

We observe that Na appears twice, note that Na has two slits
in a close position, and that this was the only slit we
could see, and that Na also has that property. so we will
assume it to be Na or sodium
